Cast · UI theme options pass · backdrops · nothing here is committed

Main-menu backdrop options

Three rough in-engine prototypes built only from existing models: the hex terrain (HexMapView + DungeonLook), the three heroes, monsters, employees, HellgateModel, priced props, decor and mail packages. The only new art is placeholder blocks (stone walls, a van stand-in, a desk). The cream panel on the left of the first image in each section is a composition mock showing where the menu sits, not a style option. The menu styles are in menus.html.

Scene: scenes/backdrop_lab.tscn. Scripts: scripts/ui/backdrop_options/. The real menu backdrop (menu_backdrop.gd) is untouched.

Backdrop 1 Recommended for the main menuprototype

The garage dawn shift in the bunker garage

The concept image, built from our parts. A stone-block garage with timber posts sits over the glowing hex floor. The van is parked on its arrival circle with the side door open. Wick, Gasket and Rebar idle around it, torches flicker, and dusty shafts fall from a ceiling grate. A hellgate glows red through a breach in the back wall, roped off with hazard tape. The signs read "24/7 EMERGENCY DISPATCH! WE FIX YOUR HEXES OR IT'S FREE!", "DAYS SINCE LAST CORN INCIDENT: 0", and a neon "CAST / WE FIX HEXES" with a dead H. The camera drifts slowly.

Cost with what we have

  • Floor, heroes, gate, barrels, crates, desk, mail and signs already exist. The prototype is about 300 lines.
  • New for real: a stone-wall kit piece (or reuse the hex walls), a torch prop, the van (in progress), and posing the crew (lean, sit, wrench-over-shoulder idles).
  • Runtime: one terrain mesh, about 6 lights, 3 models and the gate. Cheaper than a game floor.

Changes by context

  • Time of day: dawn, day or night, from the clock or the shift.
  • Last contract: stars and damages decide the mood. Good runs get a tidy garage and a cheerful crew; bad runs get scorch, smoke, corn, and the invoice pinned to the wall.
  • Corn counter: "DAYS SINCE LAST CORN INCIDENT" reads the real number.
  • Cosmetics: van paint and decals, uniforms and hats appear live, so the garage doubles as the cosmetics preview.
  • Progress: bought shop items show up on shelves; licenses hang framed.

Why it wins

  • It is the business: the crew, the van and the gate in one frame, with the tone in the signage.
  • It is a persistent "home" that remembers you, which a menu rarely does.
  • It shares its set with the van-arrival beat that starts every floor.

Watch

  • The glowing hex floor is loud under a menu, so frame it low or dim the near seams.
  • The toon shader floors brightness, so night needs a color grade, not just fewer lights.
Backdrop 2 Recommended for the job boardprototype

Site diorama the next contract as a miniature on the dispatcher's desk

A cut-out chunk of the real hex floor sits on a brass turntable on a green desk blotter and sways slowly. It is dressed as the offer's site: the client's priced props with price tags, a hellgate, a few demons, a cowering employee and the crew as tiny figures. Depth of field blurs the desk, the mug and a corkboard of job tickets behind it. On the job board it follows the highlighted offer, so the crew can see the bunker they are arguing about.

Cost with what we have

  • Almost free: every piece is an existing model. The real version could run SiteBuilder on a small radius with the offer's seed and theme.
  • New: the desk and turntable set (blocks), plus a camera with depth of field.

Changes by context

  • Swaps per highlighted offer: client, origin theme, pest and priced props.
  • Danger stars could add more demons and a hotter gate.
  • After a contract, the diorama could show the wreck with its damage tags.

Why

  • It makes the job board's text concrete, without leaving the menu.
  • A strong read on the "priced props" and "property warning" ideas.

Watch

  • Three job cards cover most of the screen, so the diorama needs a slot: behind and between the cards, or a strip.
  • As the main-menu backdrop it hides the crew; it is better as the job board's backdrop.
Backdrop 3 prototype

The storefront the business at night

A cinder-block unit on a hex-paved lot. The roll-up door is half open onto a warm shop with stocked shelves. A rooftop neon "CAST" sits over a painted board ("LICENSED BUDGET SORCERY · 1-800-LOW-MANA"), and the window has an OPEN sign and the "WE FIX YOUR HEXES" notice. The van sits in its pentagram bay ("RESERVED: VAN") under a sodium street lamp. In the foreground, an open manhole leaks red behind traffic cones while Wick eyes it: the next job is right outside.

Cost with what we have

  • Highest new-geometry cost: a building facade, a sign frame, a lamp, a skyline and a dumpster. All of it is boxes, but it is a new "outdoor" look the game never uses.

Changes by context

  • Weather, dead neon letters and the window display.
  • The "OPEN" sign turns to "CLOSED" on Clock Out.
  • The shop interior shows bought supplies.

Why

  • The most "brand" image: a great title card, trailer opener or store capsule.

Watch

  • It is outdoors and at street level, which is a different world from the bunkers the game is set in.
  • The hex floor as asphalt reads oddly.
  • Better as a title or attract screen, or the supply-house backdrop, than as the everyday menu.
Not prototyped
